newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK handover legislature adopts laws limiting rights.
newsitem.headline: HK handover legislature adopts laws limiting rights.

text.p: Hong Kong's future legislature rammed through two laws on Saturday to curb political freedoms and civil rights when China takes back the 156-year-old British colony in little more than two weeks' time.
The Provisional Legislature met across the border in the Chinese city of Shenzhen and passed amendments to two Hong Kong laws governing the freedom of association and assembly.
The changes will take effect upon the handover on July 1. The amendments were drawn up by post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa, prompted by China's National People's Congress.
A dozen or so pro-democracy activists gathered outside Tung's office in a glass tower block in Hong Kong's financial district in protest against the moves.
Under a 1984 treaty with Britain, China promised Hong Kong could keep its capitalist way of life unchanged and enjoy substantial autonomy in all but military and diplomatic matters.
But many of Hong Kong's 6.4 million people fear China will impose repressive communist-style rule, especially since the bloody 1989 anti-democracy crackdown in Beijing.
The new laws empower police to ban protests on grounds of "national security" or threats to China's territorial integrity and to disband organisations with overseas political funding.

The changes, which will curtail the rights of political parties and the rights of people to stage protest marches by setting rules on prior approval, are hotly contested by Hong Kong pro-democracy groups and by western governments -- most vocally the departing colonial power Britain.
Governor Chris Patten's spokesman was not available on Saturday to comment.

The 60-member provisional legislature, packed with pro-China politicians and tycoons, was appointed by Beijing to replace Hong Kong's elected Legislative Council when the British colony becomes an autonomous Chinese region at midnight on June 30.
Members were picked six months ago by a 400-strong selection committee tightly screened by Beijing.

Hong Kong's biggest political group, the Democratic Party, which will go into the political wilderness on July 1 when China dissolves the elected legislature, has threatened to launch court challenges to laws passed by the provisional body.
Two pro-democracy legislators in the provisional chamber, minority voices in the assembly, tried unsuccessfully to have the new legislation amended during its passage.

Former Democratic Party member Dominic Chan sought to amend the new laws so that police could only resort to "national security" as the reason for banning a protest if demonstrators were inciting foreign military intervention.
But Michael Suen, Tung's Secretary for Policy Coordination, said threats to "national security" could come without violence.

Bruce Liu from the centrist Association for Democracy and People's Livelihood, which often diverges from the official line of the future regime, sought to exempt small religious groups and charities from being registered under the new law.
But Suen maintained regristation of societies should make no distinction of size and that all organisations big and small must register with the authorities.
This is a break with past practice, as is the new requirement that parties may not enjoy foreign funding.

Suen, however, stressed that the future government, in drawing up the changes, had tried to strike a balance between civil liberties and the need for social order, an argument that is ridiculed by the pro-democracy camp who won 70 percent of the votes in direct legislative elections two years ago.
